title: The Radial Distribution Functions of Nanofluids: Molecular Dynamics Simulations
abstract: Nanofluids, which are composed of insoluble, stable, and well-dispersed solid particles of nanoscale and/or subnanometer sizes suspended in a base liquid, are the next generation of liquids of today. The purpose of this paper is to investigate the one dimensional and three dimensional angle dependent radial distribution functions RDF and ARDF of polymeric nanofluids made up of nonrigid (soft) nanoparticles and a polymer melt (base fluid) using the molecular dynamics simulation approach and to search the shape stabilities by using these results. For this purpose, we use the nanoparticles of three different sizes: 28, 42, and 56 particles. We research them both within the base fluid and without this polymeric medium for instability analysis. We found that the nanoparticles with 28 atoms show the shape instability inside the base fluid when we increase the system temperature from T=1.2 to T=1.8 and hence, the structure of two concentric spherical shell of the nanoparticle breaks down and as a result the empty vacuum between these inner and the outer shells disappears. In contrast to this findings, the nanoparticles with 42 and 56 atoms show the shape stability inside the base fluid by preserving their concentric shell structures when we rise the system temperature and decrease the affinity between the nanoparticles and the base liquid medium.
summary: This work uses Molecular Dynamics simulations to examine how nanofluids containing nonrigid nanoparticles behave structurally when suspended in a polymer melt. By analyzing radial distribution functions and mean forces, the authors determine that nanoparticle size dictates stability; specifically, smaller particles are prone to structural collapse at elevated temperatures.
main_problem: The study investigates the shape stabilities of polymeric nanofluids by analyzing their radial distribution functions (RDF/ARDF). The goal is to understand how nanoparticle structure changes under varying thermal conditions.
main_result: Nanoparticles with 28 atoms lose their concentric shell structure at higher temperatures, while those with 42 and 56 atoms maintain stability despite increasing temperature and decreasing particle-liquid affinity.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were employed using a coarse-grained particle-based approach under the NVE ensemble. The analysis focused on calculating angle-dependent radial distribution functions.
model_or_system: The system consists of nonrigid (soft) nanoparticles suspended in a polymer melt base fluid. Interactions are modeled using combinations of FENE and Lennard-Jones potentials for monomers, chains, and nanoparticle interactions.
key_observables: One dimensional and three dimensional angle dependent radial distribution functions (RDF and ARDF); Mean force magnitude as a function of relative distance.
important_parameters: Nanoparticle sizes (28, 42, and 56 atoms); Temperature range ($T=1.2$ to $T=1.8$); Interaction coefficients ($C_{mn}$).
main_assumptions: The simulation uses a coarse-grained particle-based model; the analysis assumes that changes in distribution shape reflect structural stability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate mean force calculations for 28, 42, and 56 atom nanoparticles at various interaction strengths and temperatures, showing bimodal or unimodal distributions related to shell thickness.
paper_structure: The paper details the MD simulation setup (Hamiltonian components, integration algorithms) followed by specific analyses on RDFs for stability assessment, and later analyzes mean force magnitudes as a function of relative distance across different particle sizes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical soft matter, the study's rigorous application of statistical mechanics principles to determine structural phase transitions (shape instability) under thermal stress is relevant to understanding complex many-body dynamics in confined or interacting systems.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: An illustration of the interactions inside the bulk nanofluid systems of 28, 42, and 56 particles. In the figure, three nanoparticles (each one of 28 atoms) are shown in pink colour. And also three polymer chains (each one of 10 monomers) are seen in green colour. As you can see, there are seven different interaction types based on where they occur. There are four intramolecular interactions and three intermolecular interactions. In this figure, UFENE, ULJ, and Uαβ represents FENE potential energy function, 12-6 LJ potential energy, and modified-12-6 LJ potential energy respectively.

Fig. 2: For the given values of the parameters k and R0, the variation of the component of ⃗FFENE function in the direction of unit vector ˆr with the distance r. Red vertical line represents the vertical asymptote at the point r=1.5.

Fig. 3: For six different Cαβ coefficients, modified, truncated and shifted Lennard-Jones (12,6) potential energy, Uαβ(r), as a function of the central distance r between two particles is shown. For Cαβ = 0.1, the minimum of the Uαβ(r) is approximately equal to −0.0071 at r = 1.6.

Fig. 5: Side by side visualization of spherical nanoparticles of 28 (a), 42 (b), 56 (c) atoms just after the production run of 10000τ simulation time is shown in this figure. For visualization purporse, we use VMD [40].

Figure 6 shows how the instantaneous total potential energy, Ep, the instantaneous total kinetic energy, Ek, and the instantaneous total internal energy, Ep + Ek, of the nanoparticles change with the total number of particles in a nanoparticle. When we look at the figure, we see that Ek increases linearly with the total number of particles in a nanoparticle. However, Ep +Ek and Ep increases nonlinearly with the total number of particles in a nanoparticle.
